prompt.context: Our client is a large international financial service organization. Among its many divisions, it offers commercial banking services, investment management, wealth management, treasury management services and foreign exchange. Over the past year, our client has seen a decline in RFP (requests for proposal) wins. They have hired us to figure out why and help come up with a plan to reverse this trend.
prompt.question: Why has our client seen a decline in RFP wins over the past year, and what should they do to reverse this trend?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the client's main competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Our client has 4 primary competitors of a similar size and international reach.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any new market entrants?
clarifying_info.a: While there are no new market entrants, some super-regional banks have begun to target some of our client's client segments.

clarifying_info.q: What are the client's main customer segments?
clarifying_info.a: The client has 4 main segments: Large Corporate (companies with more than $3B in annual revenue), Upper Middle Market ($500M-$3B), Lower Middle Market ($50M-$500M), and Business Banking (less than $50M annual revenue).

clarifying_info.q: Are there any notable industry trends?
clarifying_info.a: Increases in technology and ease of access to international markets have caused many firms that did not originally have international banking needs to now require such services — e.g., foreign currency options, international bank accounts, letters of credit, or other trade products.

clarifying_info.q: Is the decline in RFP wins consistent across all 4 client segments?
clarifying_info.a: (Interviewer shows Exhibit 1 — segmentation data on RFP win rates by segment over time.)

exhibits.title: RFP Win Rates by Client Segment
exhibits.shows: A chart or table showing RFP win rate trends over time broken out by the four client segments: Large Corporate, Upper Middle Market, Lower Middle Market, and Business Banking.
exhibits.data: Large Corporate: steadily increasing over the period; Business Banking: flat year over year; Upper Middle Market and Lower Middle Market: declining over the period.

exhibits.title: Product Capabilities and Pricing vs. Competition
exhibits.shows: A comparison of our client's international product capabilities and pricing relative to competitors, showing where the client stands on both dimensions.
exhibits.data: Client's product capabilities/international product offering is rated better than competitors; however, the client's pricing lies outside (above) what is perceived as acceptable to clients and is less competitive than peers.

framework: Banking Industry / Market: identify top competitors and whether they are also seeing RFP win declines; check for new entrants (e.g., super-regional banks expanding into client segments); review market segmentation; note industry trends such as the increase in technology and international banking needs among mid-market firms
Our Client: evaluate current product offering vs. competition; assess pricing relative to competition; identify any competitive advantages
Other Considerations: regulatory changes impacting the client; media or reputation issues; macroeconomic conditions; potential competitor responses to any changes the client makes

questions.prompt: Looking at the segmentation data in Exhibit 1, which segments are experiencing the RFP win decline and what does that tell you?
questions.guidance: Strong answers note that not all segments are declining. Large Corporate is steadily increasing, meaning the client does well with companies above $3B. Business Banking is flat and may not be a priority target segment. Both Middle Market segments (Upper and Lower) are declining — this is where the client should focus its investigation and response.

questions.prompt: Why might the client be seeing a decline in RFP wins specifically in the Middle Market segments?
questions.guidance: Candidate should create a structured, bucketed list of hypotheses: (1) Economic shift affecting the middle market specifically (though a true downturn would likely also hurt Business Banking); (2) Competition — clients moving to a competitor, or a competitor actively targeting the client's middle market clients; (3) Pricing — whether the client increased prices and lost competitiveness; (4) Product Offering — whether the client's products compare unfavorably to competition; (5) Other factors such as relationship quality, sales execution, or service levels.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 2 (product capabilities and pricing), what insights do you draw?
questions.guidance: The client's product capabilities and international offering are actually better than competitors — so product gaps are not the root cause. However, the client's pricing is outside the range perceived as acceptable by clients and is above competition. To be more competitive, the client can either (a) decrease price on current products, or (b) invest in additional capabilities to justify the premium. Given capabilities are already ahead of competition, investing in more capabilities is not the short-run fix.

questions.prompt: What are the risks if the client simply decreases the price of its current products?
questions.guidance: Structured bucket of risks: (1) A broad price decrease would reduce revenue across all four segments, including Large Corporate — where the client is doing well and presumably generating strong revenue at current prices; (2) Competitors may respond by also decreasing prices, potentially triggering a price war that erodes margins industry-wide; (3) Other considerations such as brand/perception damage (a price cut may signal lower quality) or difficulty raising prices again in the future.

questions.prompt: If not a simple price cut, what alternative solution would allow the client to compete in the Middle Market without hurting its Large Corporate business?
questions.guidance: The key insight is that not all segments require the same level of product sophistication. The client could develop a 'lite' version of its international products — fewer features than the full offering, but priced lower — targeted at Middle Market and even Business Banking clients. This tiered-product strategy allows the client to: (a) maintain current full-price products for Large Corporate where it is winning and margin is strong; (b) compete more effectively on price in the Middle Market; (c) avoid a broad price cut that would cannibalize Large Corporate revenue; (d) potentially capture Business Banking demand as a bonus.

brainstorming.prompt: Why might the client be losing RFP wins in the Middle Market segments specifically?

categories.name: Competitive Dynamics
ideas: A competitor is actively targeting the client's Middle Market clients
Super-regional banks entering the segment with lower-cost products
Competitors have improved their own international product suites

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Client raised prices in recent years, pushing its offering outside acceptable range for Middle Market budgets
Middle Market clients are more price-sensitive than Large Corporate clients
Client's pricing not differentiated by segment — one price for all

categories.name: Product Fit
ideas: Full-featured international products are overbuilt for Middle Market needs
Middle Market clients do not need (or want to pay for) the same capabilities as large corporates
No lighter-weight or modular product option available to Middle Market

categories.name: Sales & Relationship
ideas: Sales team focused on Large Corporate deals which are larger in size
RFP response quality or speed may be lagging in the Middle Market
Relationship managers may be undertrained on Middle Market client needs

categories.name: Macroeconomic / Structural
ideas: Middle Market firms growing into Large Corporate, shrinking the Upper Middle Market pool
Industry consolidation reducing the number of Middle Market RFPs issued
Technology platforms allowing Middle Market firms to self-serve some banking needs

recommendation: The client's decline in RFP wins is concentrated in the Middle Market segments (Upper and Lower Middle Market) and is driven primarily by a pricing mismatch — the client's products are superior to competitors, but priced above what Middle Market clients find acceptable.

The recommended solution is to develop a tiered 'lite' product offering for Middle Market (and potentially Business Banking) clients: a scaled-down version of the international product suite with fewer features but meaningfully lower pricing. This preserves Large Corporate revenue at full price while restoring competitiveness in the Middle Market.
risks: A lite product may cannibalize some Large Corporate clients if positioned or marketed broadly
Developing a new product tier requires investment in technology, operations, and sales training
Competitors may follow with their own lite offerings, compressing the pricing advantage over time
If the lite product is priced too low, it may not cover costs or may undervalue the client's brand
next_steps: Conduct detailed pricing analysis to determine the acceptable price range for Middle Market clients by sub-segment
Define the feature set for the lite product: which capabilities are valued by Middle Market vs. those that are Large Corporate-specific
Build a financial model estimating the revenue uplift from regained Middle Market RFP wins vs. the cost of product development
Pilot the lite product with a select group of Middle Market prospects before full rollout
Monitor competitor responses and be prepared to adjust pricing strategy accordingly
